title: Supplemental Lighting & DLI in Greenhouses
summary: Greenhouse crops receive changing amounts of natural photosynthetic light across the day and season. Supplemental lighting should be evaluated as part of total daily light integral, canopy distribution, photoperiod, energy use, and crop response rather than as a fixed fixture setting.
keyConcepts: DLI integrates photosynthetic photon flux over time
Greenhouse glazing, structure, season, cloud cover, and shade reduce or redistribute natural light
Supplemental lighting can fill a light deficit but also adds heat and electrical load
A crop-level light plan should distinguish total light quantity from photoperiod signaling
measureObserve: Measure or log DLI at crop height in representative zones
Map PPFD from both sunlight and fixtures at several times or conditions
Record fixture schedules and dimming state
Track crop response alongside total daily light and temperature
commonMistakes: Using one instantaneous PPFD reading as the daily light total
Ignoring seasonal changes in natural greenhouse light
Adding light without checking heat load and canopy uniformity
Treating a DLI target from another crop or system as universal

title: Photoperiod Integrity, Blackout & Light Leaks
summary: Photoperiod-sensitive flowering depends on the timing and duration of light and darkness. Protected structures can introduce unintended night lighting from fixtures, work lights, nearby buildings, incomplete blackout, or control failures.
keyConcepts: Photoperiod is a timing signal separate from total DLI
Night interruption can alter photoperiod responses in sensitive plants
Blackout systems must control light while still accounting for heat, humidity, and airflow
Timers, sensors, curtains, and human activity can all create schedule failures
measureObserve: Audit the structure during the intended dark period
Check curtain edges, doors, vents, indicator lights, and neighboring light sources
Record actual fixture and blackout schedules rather than assumed schedules
Inspect temperature and RH changes after blackout closure
commonMistakes: Assuming a closed curtain means complete darkness
Ignoring work lights and equipment indicators
Closing blackout without planning for heat and humidity buildup
Changing photoperiod and light quantity at the same time without documenting both
